Paleomagnetism of the Ulkan massif (SE Siberian platform) and the
apparent polar wander path for Siberia in late Paleoproterozoic–early
Mesoproterozoic times
A.N. Didenkoa,c,∗, V.Yu. Vodovozovb,c, A.Yu. Peskova, V.A. Guryanova, A.V. Kosynkina
aKosygin Institute of Tectonics and Geophysics, Far Eastern Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences, 65 Kim Yu Chen Str., Khabarovsk 680000, Russia
bFaculty of Geology, Lomonosov Moscow State University, 1 Leninskie Gory, Moscow 119234, Russia
cGeological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, 7 Pyzhevsky lane, Moscow 119017, Russia

Ulkan
a
massif
b s t r a c t
Paleomagnetic studies on Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Ulkan massif from the south-eastern Siberian plat-
form yielded two ancient paleomagnetic directions and made it possible to calculate poles corresponding
to them for two time intervals in the late Paleoproterozoic: (ɑ) ∼1732 Ma for volcanogenic-sedimentary
rocks of the Elgetey Formation – Plat = 7.1◦(−7.1◦), Plong = 183.5◦(3.5◦), dp= 10.5◦, dm= 16.4◦(positive
fold, reversals and conglomerates tests); and (b) less than 1720 Ma for granites of the Ulkan Complex –
Plat = 42.1◦(−42.1◦), Plong = 249.4◦(69.4◦), dp= 3.4◦, dm= 5.6◦. The analysis of the existing paleomagnetic
data for Siberia in late Paleoproterozoic–early Mesoproterozoic times allowed a total of 12 new poles to
be defined with five of them considered key poles (Table 3), based on which the APWP for Siberia was
generated. On the basis of the data presented here, one can conclude that in the context of the Paleo-
proterozoic supercontinent model, preference is given to the position of Paleoproterozoic north poles of
Siberia in the Indian Ocean and Australia, rather than in the Atlantic Ocean.
© 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
The Siberian (East Siberian) platform of Precambrian age
(Fig. 1a), which is almost 4.5 million km2in area, occurs at the cen-
tre of the Central Asia structure. In the north, east and south it
is bounded by the Novaya Zemlya–Taimyr, Verkhoyansk–Kolyma
and Mongol–Okhotsk Phanerozoic fold belts, respectively, and in
the west by the young West Siberian platform. The structure of
the Siberian platform basement is asymmetric. Early Precambrian
structures are widespread in its southern part: the Aldan–Stanovoy
shield dominates the south-east of the platform; the Akitkan
volcano-plutonic belt and the Sharyzhalgai salient are dominant in
the south; and the Angar–Kan volcano-plutonic belt and the Yeni-
sei ridge are located in the south-west and west. In the northern
part of the platform, these structures occur only within the Anabar
massif (shield) and a small part of the Olenek uplift. Meso- and Neo-
proterozoic sedimentary formations which are divided into two
∗

680000, Russia. Tel.: +7 4212227189; fax: +7 4212227189.
E-mail address: itig@itig.as.khb.ru (A.N.
structural
Didenko).
stages are widely developed within the Siberian platform
along with the Phanerozoic sedimentary cover.
At the end of the last century, a number of authors (Borukaev,
1985; Zonenshain et al., 1990; Tectonics, 1988; Rosen et al., 1994)
put forward a model of the Siberian craton formation within the
context of the terrane concept, which is based on differences in
geological structure of individual blocks of the craton as well as
petrological and geochronological data: Angar–Anabar, Tunguska,
Olenek, Aldan and Stanovoy (Fig. 1b). According to Zonenshain et al.
(1990), Rosen et al. (2006) and Tectonics (2001), prior to ∼1.9 Ga
there was no single Siberian craton – the above five terranes were
separated by the ocean basins. At the end of the Paleoproterozoic
they formed two distinct cratons: one encompassing Aldan and
Stanovoy terranes, and the second, formed by the collision of the
Angar–Anabar, Tunguska and Olenek terranes.
Borukaev (Tectonics, 1988), and later Zonenshain et al. (1990)
and Rosen et al. (2006), related the Akitkan and Bilyakchan–Ulkan
(Ulkan) volcano-plutonic belts to the major structural sutures that
joined terranes of the Siberian craton in the Paleo-Mesoproterozoic
(Fig. 1b). The latter are identified by Zonenshain et al. (1990) with
continental-margin volcanic arcs. The wide occurrence of such
structures in all cratons of the Earth allowed Borukaev (1985) to
categorize them as Akitkan-type structures.

0301-9268/© 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

### page_2
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 59
Fig. 1. The Siberian platform in the World (a) and General tectonic scheme of the Siberian craton (b) according to Rosen and Fedorovsky (2001) and Rosen et al. (2006).
Terranes: BT – Batomga, CG – Chogar, NM – Nimnyr, SU – Sutam, TN – Tynda, UC – Uchur, and WA – West Aldan.
In his comprehensive review, Khain (2001) considers the Ulkan
trough, as well as Bilyakchan and Udokan ones, to be created by rift-
ing. According to him, rifting began ∼2.2 Ga ago with the formation
of the Udokan depression filled in with a thick series of continental-
clastic red beds and granitoids of the Kodar–Kemen Complex and
spread eastward (in present-day coordinates) into the Ulkan and
Bilyakchan troughs. Originally it was Berezhnaya et al. (1988) who
estimated the age of the Chiney sub-Group of the Udokan Group
as 2.18 Ga. There is an alternative opinion as to the genesis of the
Udokan–Chiney structures – transition of the passive continental
margin into an active one (Abramov, 2007).
According to Larin (2008), whose view is conformable with
the above but different in the timing of rifting, the Ulkan struc-
ture formed “. . . under the conditions of lithospheric stretching in
within-plate environments . . . of active rifting due to large-scale
upwelling of hot mantle beneath the growing Nuna superconti-
nents (1.75–1.70 Ga)”. Later on this view was developed in Larin
(2009) and Larin et al. (2012). There is also a link with the ca.
1750 Ma radiating dyke swarm of Gladkochub et al. (2010) which
is focused on the eastern end of the Akitkan belt.
It is shown in Kotov (2003), Rosen and Fedorovsky (2001), Rosen
et al. (2006), Smelov and Timofeev (2003) and Tectonics (2001)
the
that
Aldan–Stanovoy shield consists of a number of terranes varying
in in-filling (West Aldan, Batomga, Tynda, Nimnyr, Chogar, Sutam,
and Uchur; Fig. 1b), separated by the zones of tectonic melange
(Kalar, Amga, and Tyrkanda). Complexes that “suture” them, includ-
ing anorthosites, are developed within these zones and some
terranes (Tectonics, 2001). Anorthosites of the Dzhugdzhur massif,
which are part of the anorogenic Bilyakchan–Ulkan volcano-
plutonic belt, “suture” the Early Precambrian tectonic structures
of the south-eastern Siberian platform, and the observed structure
of the Aldan–Stanovoy shield took shape in the second half of the
Paleoproterozoic (Tectonics, 2001).
To date reliable paleomagnetic data on Tunguska and Anabar
provinces of the Siberian craton have been published for the second
half of the Paleoproterozoic and Mesoproterozoic, which made it
possible to develop the first apparent polar wander path (APWP)
for Siberia for this time interval (Didenko et al., 2009a,b; Veselovsky
et al., 2009; Vodovozov et al., 2011). Up to now, there have been
no reliable paleomagnetic data on this age interval for Aldan and
Stanovoy provinces of the Siberian craton.
This paper deals with the following issues: (1) presentation of
the first paleomagnetic data on the upper Paleoproterozoic rocks
of the Aldan–Stanovoy province; (2) comparison of the defined

### page_3
60 A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77
Fig. 2. Geological sketch-map of the Ulkan massif (trough) and the adjacent territory of the Siberian platform.
paleomagnetic poles with paleomagnetic data on Tunguska and
Anabar provinces (Didenko et al., 2009a,b; Vodovozov et al., 2011),
and (3) presentation of a new model of the APWP for Siberia for the
second half of the Paleoproterozoic and early Mesoproterozoic.
2. Brief geologic setting of the study area
Structures of the Ulkan massif occur on the south-eastern edge
of the Aldan terrane (Fig. 1b) in the upper reaches of Uchur,
Toporikan, Ulkan, and Nimar (Fig. 2). Paleoproterozoic unmetamor-
phosed rocks here (sedimentary-volcanogenic rocks of the Ulkan
Group and granitoids of the Ulkan Complex) are overlain by Meso-
proterozoic deposits of the platform cover and rest with angular
unconformity on metamorphic rocks of the Aldan–Stanovoy shield
and their weathering crust (Fig. 3) thus marking the time of con-
solidation of the Siberian platform crystalline basement.
Alekseev et al. (1962) were the first to distinguish the Ulkan
Group within Toporikan and Elgetey Formations. Later on its
composition and volume were repeatedly revised by different
authors; in this study V.A. Guryanov’s stratigraphic scheme is used
(Guryanov, 2007; Didenko et al., 2010; Guryanov et al., 2012), under
which the group comprises Toporikan, Ulkachan and Elgetey For-
mations whose total thickness is over 3 km (Fig. 3). Subvolcanic
intrusions and vent extrusions make up a large part of the group
(Fig. 2) which together with lava flows are considered as Ulkachan
trachybasalt and Elgetey basalt–trachyrhyolite volcanic complexes.
The Elgetey Formation which is over 2 km thick and divided into
three sub-formations (Fig. 3) occurs at the top of the Ulkan Group. It
is dominated by red trachyrhyolites, trachyrhyodacites and trachy-
dacites. There also occur their tuffs, ignimbrites and lava breccias,
pantellerites and comendites; less common are mafic lavas. Sedi-
mentary and tuffaceous-sedimentary rocks occur in lava flows as
rare interbeds and layers. The Elgetey Formation, as a rule, rests
unconformable either on the Ulkachan or Toporikan Formation,
and outside of these occurrences, it overlies the crystalline base-
ment. According to Larin (2008), the age of trachyrhyolites in the
Elgetey Formation is assessed at 1720 + 2.5 Ma (U–Pb method on
zircons). According to our data (Didenko et al., 2013), the concord-
ant age of zircons (U–Pb) from the Upper Elgetey
is
sub-Formation
1732 ± 4 Ma (analyses were carried out by E.B. Salnikova and
A.B. Kotov in the Laboratory of Isotope Geology at the Institute of
Geochemistry and Precambrian Geology, RAS).
Granitoids of the Ulkan alkaline–leucogranite complex make
up two large massifs and several small- and mid-size intrusions,
which are exposed in different parts of the Ulkan trough and its
framing (Fig. 2). The largest two massifs are Ulkan and South
Uchur, the former being petrotypical. Ulkan granitoids intruded in
three consecutive phases: 1st phase with an age of 1729.7 ± 1.9 Ma
(U–Pb zircon) – subalkaline granites and biotite leucogranites,
quartz syenites, monzonites, and syenite porphiries; 2nd phase –
subalkaline biotite fine-grained leucogranites; 3rd phase with an
age of 1724 ± 3.6 Ma (U–Pb zircon) – alkaline granites and quartz
aegirine-riebeckite syenites (Didenko et al., 2010). Analytical stud-
ies were carried out under the direction of E.V. Bibikova in the
Laboratory of Isotope Geochemistry and Geochronology at Vernad-
sky Institute of Geochemistry and Analytical Chemistry, RAS.
According to Neymark et al. (1992) and (Larin et al., 1997),
zircons from first, second and third phase granites of the
Ulkan Complex are dated at 1720.8 ± 1.0, 1715.8 ± 2.5 and
1704.6 ± 4.7 Ma (U–Pb zircon), respectively.
Sediments of the lower Mesoproterozoic Uyan Group rest with
angular unconformity on rocks of the Elgetey Formation (Fig. 3).
The significance of this break is highlighted by the development of
the ferruginous–clay–hydromicaceous weathering crust with the
Rb–Sr isochron age of 1670 ± 40 Ma (Guryanov, 2007; Kazakov and
Knorre, 1973) underlying the Birindya Formation (bottom of the
Uyan Group).
To resolve contradictions among the existing models a detailed
paleomagnetic study of the Ulkan Group volcanics and the Ulkan
massif granites was conducted at eight sites within its central part
(Fig. 2; mean coordinates: 56.25◦N, 134.67◦E).
3. Paleomagnetic studies
3.1. Paleomagnetic research techniques
Field and laboratory paleomagnetic studies and data
processing were carried out mainly by standard procedures

### page_4
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 61
Fig. 3. The Ulkan Group in the Precambrian section of the south-eastern Siberian platform.
(Paleomagnetology, 1982; Pechersky and Didenko, 1995; Butler,
1992; Van der Voo, 1990). Sampling for rock magnetic and pale-
omagnetic measurements was preceded by measuring the initial
magnetic susceptibility (k) directly in outcrops using a Czeck field
magnetic susceptibility metre KT-5 (sensitivity of 1 × 10−5S.I.
units). Fine-grained sediments, fine-grained granites, and igneous
rocks with k of moderate magnitude were our first choice. During
igneous rock sampling the preference was given to quench zones
which were recognized both visually and by a regular decline
in k values from the centre of bodies outwards. In laboratory
conditions, measurements of k for all the samples were repeated
using a Czech magnetic susceptibility metre MFK-1FA (sensitivity
of 5 × 10−8S.I. units).
A magnetic compass was used for sample and bedding element
orientation and magnetic declination was taken into account when
determining mean paleomagnetic directions. Rock samples were
cut into 2 cm cubes in the laboratory using a diamond saw.
To estimate the age of the natural remanent magnetization
(NRM) in rock samples we have succeeded in applying the intrafor-
mational conglomerate test, unfortunately, in a strongly reduced
form, for rocks of the lower sub-formation of the Elgetey Forma-
tion as well as fold and reversal tests. We failed to apply any direct
field tests for granitoids of the Ulkan Complex.
Magnetic parameters which characterize the structure, concen-
tration, and carriers of magnetism were examined using a number
of representative samples of the studied rocks. Initial and repeated
temperature dependences of saturation magnetization (Ms) were
primarily studied to determine the Curie point (Tc) and the sta-
bility of magnetization carriers to heating. All the samples
subjected
were
to the complete stepwise thermal demagnetization up
to 570–670◦C in the furnace with the four-layer permalloy shiel-
ding (the magnetic field in the furnace was less than 15–20 nT). Each
time samples were heated their position in the furnace was changed
randomly to decrease the impact of laboratory magnetizing. A heat-
ing step depended on the behaviour of magnetization in the study
and varied progressively from 50 to 100◦C at low temperatures to
20–30◦C at medium temperatures and to 5–10◦C at high tempera-
tures. Usually the number of thermal cleaning steps ranged from 15
to 20. NRM studies were done with a Czech spinner magnetome-
ter JR-6a (bulk magnetic moment sensitivity is 2.4 × 10−6A/m)
mounted in the Helmholtz coils. Samples were transferred from
the furnace to the measuring instrument in the (cid:2)-metal container.
The data set obtained by demagnetization was analyzed using
the PMGSC software v.4.2 (Enkin, 2004). This software com-
prises standard tools for processing, displaying and analysing
palaeomagnetic data, including principal component analysis
(PCA; Kirschvink, 1980) and remagnetization circle analysis (RCA;
McFadden and McElhinny, 1988). The fold test was performed using
the PMGSC software (Enkin, 2004) and reversal tests (McFadden
and McElhinny, 1990). T. Torsvik’s GMAP software was used
(Torsvik and Smethurst, 1999) to trace tectonic block movements
on the sphere and to generate apparent polar wander paths
(APWPs).
3.2. Magnetization carriers of the studied rocks
The Ms-T dependence of the studied, more magnetic rocks, such
as samples of trachydacite of the Elgetey Formation (Fig. 4a) and

### page_5
62 A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77
Fig. 4. Magnetic mineralogy. Saturation magnetization vs. temperature (a–e).
rapakivi-granite (Fig. 4b), takes a single-phase form with Curie
points between 578◦C and 605◦C. Curie points are well defined on
the second derivative curves of Ms-T dependences of these samples
– a typical “kink” in the above temperature range. These samples
exhibit a high stability to the laboratory heating to 700◦C. First,
Ms values before and after heating are almost equal; second, Curie
points when reheated have the same values (Fig. 4a). Behaviour
of rapakivi samples when heated in the laboratory is somewhat
different: there is a small (10–25%) decrease in Ms values
heating,
after
and when reheated, along with the first magnetic phase
identified at the first heating, there is a second magnetic phase
with haematite temperatures (Fig. 4b). A decrease in Ms after heat-
ing and the occurrence of hematite at repeated heating testify that
some cation-deficient magnetite (Tc ≈ 605◦C) changes to hematite
(Tc ≈ 675◦C).
Among volcanics of the Elgetey Formation there occur spec-
imens with two-phase magnetic structure, which is inherent,
mainly, in acid varieties (Fig. 4c). The first magnetic phase of the

### page_6
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 63
Fig. 5. Natural remanence magnetization (NRM) vs. magnetic susceptibility (k), and its distribution.
trachyrhyolite sample corresponds to the cation-deficient mag-
netite with Tc ∼ 590◦C and the second – to hematite (Tc ∼ 670◦C).
Both of these magnetic phases are clearly seen on Ms-T depen-
dences of the first and second heating. Ms of such samples decreases
appreciably after the first heating to 50–70% of the initial value
(Fig. 4c). We believe this is related to the transition of a portion
of the cation-deficient magnetite to hematite during laboratory
heating.
The third type of the igneous rocks studied is their weakly mag-
netic varieties with an almost hyperbolic appearance of the Ms-T
dependence. As an example we refer to Fig. 4d which presents
the Ms-T dependence of the 2nd phase alkaline feldspathic gran-
ite of the Ulkan Complex. The figure shows that following the first
and the second heating a small magnetic phase with Tc close to
magnetite (a gentle kink on the second derivative curves of Ms-T
relationship for the sample) stands out against the background of
the paramagnetic phase. Samples with extremely low concentra-
tion of ferromagnetic minerals (a few hundredths of a percent) are
characterized by paramagnetic-type curves.
The Ms-T dependence of the studied sedimentary rocks of the
Elgetey Formation has practically the same shape. As an exam-
ple we referred to the Ms-T dependence for the fine-grained
quartz-feldspar sandstone (Fig. 4e), wherein magnetic minerals are
presented by two phases: the first either by magnetite or cation-
deficient magnetite and the second by hematite. Both of these
magnetic phases are recorded on Ms-T dependences of the first and
the second heating. Ms of sediment samples following the first heat-
ing remains essentially unchanged (Fig. 4d), suggesting the stability
of the Elgetey sediments to laboratory heating.
Values of initial magnetic susceptibility (k) and natural rema-
nent magnetization (NRM) of the studied specimens vary within
a wide range (Fig. 5) – more than three orders of magnitude:
k from 3 × 10−5 to 5 × 10−2S.I. units, NRM from 2 × 10−4 to
1 A/m. The distribution of these values is non-monotonic and
non-unimodal, analysis of the NRM-k chart and their
suggests
distributions
three groups of samples (Fig. 5): strongly magnetic
(NRM > 8 × 10−2A/m, k > 3 × 10−3S.I. units), moderately magnetic
(5 × 10−3< NRM < 8 × 10−2A/m, 1 × 10−4< k < 3 × 10−3S.I. units)
and weakly magnetic (NRM < 5 × 10−3A/m, k < 1 × 10−4S.I. units).
We believe that such a significant variation of k is, first of all,
due to differences in concentrations of ferrimagnetic minerals in
these samples, whereas the value of NRM depends not only on the
concentration of magnetic minerals, but also on their structural
features – the linear correlation coefficient of these two variables
is 0.74. The group of strongly magnetic samples comprises mafic
volcanics of the Elgetey Formation. The moderately magnetic min-
eral group comprises all the studied felsic and a portion of mafic
volcanics of the Elgetey Formation as well as rapakivi-type gran-
ites. And the weakly magnetic mineral group comprises alkaline
feldspathic granites and sediments of the Elgetey Formation.
The Köningsberger ratio (Qn) of the studied samples varies
within a wide range: from 0.05 to 20 for the felsic and a portion
of mafic volcanics of the Elgetey Formation, and from 0.035 to 4 for
the rapakivi-type granites (Fig. 5). A significant proportion of gran-
ites and volcanics of the Elgetey Formation have Qn> 1, suggesting
the predominance of the remanent magnetization over the induced
magnetization in these rocks, on the one hand, and their magnetic
rigidity, on the other. The latter fact is favourable for preserving the
ancient remanent magnetization.
3.3. Paleomagnetic characteristics of granitoids
Results of thermal demagnetization up to 600–620◦C of 120
granitoid samples of the Ulkan Complex are given in Table 1 and
Fig. 6. The NRM behaviour of 27 samples during their stepwise
thermal cleaning is unstable and will not be analyzed further. This
behaviour is characteristic of extremely magnetically soft speci-
mens with Qn< 0.1 (Fig. 5). The NRM behaviour of the remaining
93 samples during thermal magnetic cleaning is interpretable. At
least 2–3 paleomagnetic components are normally isolated from

each sample. The direction of a high-temperature component (HTC)
was resolved for 69 of the 93 samples by principal component anal-
ysis (PCA) and for 24 samples by circles of remagnetization. As an
example we can refer to the results of thermal demagnetization of
three granite samples (Fig. 6) on the orthogonal Zijderveld diagrams
(Zijderveld, 1967).
An almost perfect Zijederveld plot was constructed for sample
D08/08-1a (Fig. 6a). Here two components are isolated, the direc-
tion of the low-temperature component (LTC), isolated by three
points from 20 to 250◦C (Dec = 132◦, Inc = 21◦), being different from
the direction of the present-day geomagnetic field in the study area.
The NRM high-temperature component of the sample (Dec = 62◦,
Inc = 18◦) is isolated by seven points between 460◦C and 610◦C
and passes through the origin.
Sample D08/07-16b (Fig. 6b) exhibits a more complex behaviour
of NRM during thermal magnetic cleaning: (a) the LTC (Dec =
Inc
7◦,
= 67◦) being in rough agreement with the direction of the
present-day geomagnetic field, is isolated between 20◦C and
200◦C; (b) a smooth inflection is observed then to temperatures
350◦C–400◦C; and (c) the HTC is separated by six points between
420◦C and 570◦C and its direction is Dec = 227◦, Inc = −46◦. When
directions of HTCs of this and the previous sample are compared,
it is evident that they are different in polarity. There are but three
samples for which such a component is isolated (third quadrant
and negative inclination), whereas the number of samples with the
opposite direction of the HTC (first quadrant and positive inclina-
tion) is significantly higher, that is, 66.
Among granitoid samples there is also a third group, for which
the HTC can be isolated only by the circles of remagnetization.
An example shows the NRM behaviour of sample D08/20-5a dur-
ing thermal magnetic cleaning (Fig. 6c): (a) the LTC (Dec = 13◦,
Inc = 48◦) being very close in its direction to the direction of the

### page_8
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 65
present-day geomagnetic field, is isolated between 20 and 300◦C;
(b) then, against the background of some scattering on the great
circle arc there is a regular arrangement of vectors during cleaning
to 560◦C (direction of the normal to the plane of the great circle is
Dec = 221◦, Inc = +59◦). A total of 24 granitoid samples exhibit such
behaviour.
Table 1 gives site-mean directions of NRM high-temperature
components of granitoids of the Ulkan Complex as well as their
distribution on the stereogram (Fig. 6d and e). Directions of the
HTC both by samples (Fig. 6d) and their site-mean (Fig. 6e) are well
grouped around the general mean with Dec = 47–48◦, Inc = 38–39◦;
the results of various options for calculating the mean direction
of the component are being essentially the same (Table 1). We
define this direction as characteristic for granites of the Ulkan Com-
plex. The paleomagnetic pole calculated by the mean direction for
93 samples and used by us in subsequent constructions has the
coordinates: Plat = −42.1◦(+42.1◦), Plong = 69.4◦(249.4◦), dp= 3.4◦,
dm= 5.6◦.
3.4. Paleomagnetic characteristics of rocks of the Elgetey
Formation
More than 260 oriented rock samples of the Elgetey Formation
have undergone thermal demagnetization, the results of which are
presented in Table 2 and Figs. 7 and 8. To substantiate the paleo-
magnetic reliability of the isolated characteristic magnetization for
the rocks of the formation only one test has been carried out to full
extent, that is, a fold test, while the other two types, conglomerate
and reversal tests, were carried out in a somewhat reduced form.
3.4.1. Conglomerate test
The intraformational conglomerate test was performed on a
small number of samples. This is due, firstly, to the small size of
pebbles in the studied exposure of conglomerates, and, secondly, to
their strongly weathered condition which resulted in their crum-
bling when cut. Only 6 pebble samples were fully demagnetized
thermally. Fig. 7a gives a Zijderveld plot for sample D-09/07-
6a; two components are isolated here. The direction of the NRM
low-temperature component is Dec = 26◦, Inc = 64◦ in geographic
coordinates, which is close to the direction of the present-day
geomagnetic field in the study area; that of the HTC is Dec = 16◦,
Inc = −14◦ and it is isolated between 460◦C and 595◦C by seven
points and passes through the origin.
The test of pebbles from the intraformational conglomerates
yielded the following results (Table 2): (1) the LTC mean direction is
Dec = 346◦, Inc = 56◦in geographic coordinates and the normalized
resultant vector is 0.872; (2) the HTC mean direction is Dec = 10◦,
Inc = −27◦ with the normalized resultant vector of 0.605; and (3)
the critical value of the normalized resultant vector for a set of six
samples is 0.642 (Shipunov, 2000). Thus, the conglomerates test for
the NRM low-temperature component can be thought of as negative
and that for the high-temperature component as positive. Notice
that six samples are not enough for a full test.
3.4.2. Thermomagnetic cleaning oriented samples of the Elgetey
Formation
The NRM behaviour of sediments and volcanics of the Elgetey
Formation during thermal cleaning is different. Samples are com-
bined into four groups as a matter of convenience in presenting the
data.
1. Samples with a single-component NRM, the component being
observed in two options of polarity: (ɑ) the fine-grained sand-
stone sample from the bottom of the upper sub-formation of
the Elgetey Formation – Dec = 161◦, Inc = 26◦ (Fig. 7b); (b) the
trachyrhyolite sample from the flows overlying the
–
sediments
Dec = 324◦, Inc = −42◦ (Fig. 7c); and (c) the trachydacite sam-
ple from the lower sub-formation of the Elgetey Formation
– Dec = 130◦, Inc = 38◦ (Fig. 7d). In the latter case, the NRM
behaviour is more “noisy”, the accuracy of resolving the com-
ponent direction is 8◦, whereas in the first two cases – 2◦.
2. Samples whose NRM is a sum of two and more components:
(ɑ) the trachydacite sample from the lower sub-formation of
the Elgetey Formation with LTC (Dec = 35◦, Inc = +36◦) and HTC
(Dec = 316◦, Inc = −27◦) (Fig. 7e); and (b) the trachydacite sample
from the same part of the section with LTC (Dec = 36◦, Inc = +71◦),
MTC (Dec = 239◦, Inc = −59◦) and HTC (Dec = 327◦, Inc = −17◦)
(Fig. 7f).
3. A large group of samples whose NRM high-temperature com-
ponent is isolated by the circles of remagnetization. As an
example we refer to the Zijderveld plot and the stereogram
with the distribution of vectors during thermal cleaning of sam-
ple D08/15-3-1b (Fig. 7g). The LTC with Dec = 128◦, Inc = +70◦is
clearly defined on the Zijderveld plot, while the HTC does not
“migrate” towards the origin. The vectors of the stereogram char-
acterizing the latter lie on the arc of the great circle the normal
to the plane of which is Dec = 238◦, Inc = 19◦.
4. The last group comprises samples whose NRM has a significant
proportion of the component (until complete demagnetization)
of a similar direction as the characteristic magnetization of gran-
itoids of the Ulkan Complex (see below). As an example, Fig. 7h
presents a diagram of the sample from the basalt flow of the
lower sub-formation of the Elgetey Formation whose HTC direc-
tion is Dec = 26◦, Inc = 26◦. Samples of this group with the NRM
direction close to the “granite direction” were excluded from
further analysis.
3.4.3. Fold test
Table 2 and Fig. 8 present site-mean directions of the NRM
high-temperature component of the first three groups of rocks of
the Elgetey Formation which yielded the “non-granite” direction.
Analysis of distributions in stratigraphic (Fig. 8b) and geographic
(Fig. 8a) coordinates of individual HTC directions at the sample
level and of mean directions at the site-mean level showed a signif-
icant increase in grouping in the stratigraphic system. In the case
of statistics at the sample level, Ks/Kg = 2.14, at the site-mean level,
Ks/Kg = 2.53 (Table 2). The best grouping is achieved at 108 ± 12%
stepwise unfolding (Fig. 8c) suggesting the predominance of the
pre-folding “pre-granite” component in the NRM of the rocks of the
Elgetey Formation.
3.4.4. Reversal test
The “pre-granite” age of the isolated HTC is supported by the fact
that the HTC direction of samples from site D08/12 (Table 2) differs
by almost 180◦ from the mean directions of other five sites. Even
though the observed value ((cid:2) obs= 7.8◦) and the value critical for
this set of samples ((cid:2) t
cri
= 39.9◦) differ essentially between direc-
tions of the two polarities due to the insufficient number of samples
with the reverse component, the reversals test is characterized as
indeterminate (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990). For purposes of
further interpretation, the HTC mean direction of all the samples
in the stratigraphic system is used as characteristic ancient mag-
netization of rocks of the Elgetey Formation: Dec = 115◦, Inc = 42◦
(Table 2). The paleomagnetic pole calculated based on this direc-
tion has the coordinates: Plat = −7.4◦(+7.4◦), Plong = 10.5◦(195.5◦),
dp= 3.8◦, dm= 6.2◦.

remanence direction. For other designations see Table 1.
600◦C is the main carrier of magnetization among granitoids of the
Ulkan Complex; (2) magnetite, cation-defficient magnetite with
Curie points between 590 and 610◦C and occasionally hematite
are the main carriers of magnetization among volcanics of the
Elgetey Formation; (3) studied samples were characterized by sta-
ble behaviour (without newly formed magnetic minerals) when
heated to 600–700◦C; and (4) a major part of samples of granitoids
and volcanics alike have Qn> 1, that is, they are magnetically rigid
enough to maintain magnetization with time.
The main criteria for the quality of paleomagnetic data used
to solve tectonics problems are (Pechersky and Didenko, 1995;
Van der Voo, 1990): (1) a sufficient number of independently ori-
ented samples and satisfactory statistical distribution parameters
of interpretable magnetization vectors of the sample collection; (2)
full and detailed demagnetization accompanied by PCA; (3) posi-
tive tests of paleomagnetic stability; (4) a well-defined age of rocks
and correspondence of one of the NRM components to this age; (5)
structural control of the studied rocks and their tectonic similarity
(coherence) to the craton or other tectonic block under study; and
(6) no evidence of regional remagnetization. The information on the
first three criteria for the resolved ancient paleomagnetic directions
is given in the previous section, the last three criteria as applied to
the granites of the Ulkan Complex and sedimentary-volcanogenic
rocks of the Elgetey Formation are discussed below.
No special research on the thermal history of the Ulkan Com-
plex granites has been carried out but judging by the cooling rates
of granitoid intrusions of the Shumikha Complex (Didenko et
2005),
al.,
which have a similar size and are classified as A-type as well
as by other estimates of cooling rates for granite intrusions, granites
had to pass the threshhold of 578◦C (the Curie point for magnetite)
within 5–10 Myr after the closure of the U–Pb (−750◦C) isotopic
system in zircons. The literature suggests that the cooling rate of
granite intrusions in this temperature range (750–300◦C) can be
11◦/Ma (Shen et al., 2000) and from 30◦/Ma early in the cooling
process to 10◦/Ma at the close of the cooling (Pitcher, 1997).
According to the previously published geochronological data
on granites of the Ulkan Complex (Neymark et al., 1992; Larin
et al., 1997), the age of zircons from first-, second- and third-phase
granites of the Ulkan Complex is 1720.8 ± 1.0, 1715.8 ± 2.5 and
1704.6 ± 4.7 Ma, respectively. The age of the Ulkan Complex gran-
ites from our data (Didenko et al., 2010) is 1729.7 ± 1.9 Ma (1st
phase) and 1724.7 ± 3.6 Ma (3rd phase). We assume that the age
of the NRM high-temperature component of the Ulkan Complex
granitoids should be less than 1720 Ma at an average rate of their
cooling of about 20◦/Ma.
The second important issue for the subsequent interpretation
of the paleomagnetic direction for granitoids, and which requires a
comment, is the assumption of the hypothesis of no significant rota-
tion of the Ulkan massif about the horizontal axis after the intrusion
of granitoids. Sediments of the lower Proterozoic Uyan Group rest
on rocks of the Elgetey Formation, granitoids of the Ulkan Com-
plex and their weathering crust with Rb-Sr age of 1670 ± 40 Ma
(Guryanov, 2007) (Fig. 3). Ulkan deposits accumulated in the inland
basin in the fluvial-deltaic, littoral and sublittoral sedimentary

### page_11
68 A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77
Fig. 8. Stereographic projection in situ (a) and tilt-corrected (b) for selected site mean directions for the Elgetey Formation, and statistical results from stepwise unfolding
(c; calculated after Enkin, 2004). Solid (open) symbols are upper (lower) hemisphere on stereogram. Star denotes the mean direction.
environments (Khudoley et al., 2001) are characterized by gentle,
almost horizontal bedding (Karsakov et al., 2002; Semikhatov and
Serebrjakov, 1983). Thus, there are reasons to assume that granit-
oids had no rotations about the horizontal axis after 1670 Ma.
The concordant age of zircons from the Upper Elgetey sub-
Formation (Didenko et al., 2013) was previously estimated as
1732 ± 4 Ma. Based on the above data on the HTC paleomagnetic
stability of rocks in the formation, its age can be characterized
as pre-folding and “pre-granite”, i.e. ∼1732 Ma, which is close to
the age of rocks from the upper sub-formation of the Elgetey
Formation.
5. A new APW path for Siberia at the end of the
Paleoproterozoic–beginning of the Mesoproterozoic
The first version of the APWP for Siberia at the end of the
Paleoproterozoic (Didenko et al., 2009a,b) was developed solely
on the basis of our own new paleomagnetic data on Akitkan and
North Baikal ridges, Sharyzhalgai and Angar–Kan salients of the
Siberian platform. Then (Veselovsky et al., 2009; Vodovozov, 2010;
Vodovozov et al., 2011) came up with new versions of the APWP for
Siberia at the end of the Paleoproterozoic–Mesoproterozoic involv-
ing data on the Anabar Massif, Olenek uplift, and Aldan–Stanovoy
shield. And new data on the Ulkan massif (SE of the Aldan–Stanovoy
shield) prompted us to turn again to the issue of defining the APWP
for Siberia at the end of the Paleoproterozoic–beginning of
5.1.
the
Mesoproterozoic.
Analysis of the available data and generation of the APWP
A total of 31 independent palemagnetic measurements for
Siberia were obtained while reviewing GPDB-4.6 (Pisarevsky, 2005)
and newly published results (Veselovskiy, 2006; Veselovsky et al.,
2009) for the above indicated time interval (Table 3). Some of
the measurements were made on rocks of the same formations
but, except the Kotuikan Formation of the Anabar massif, their
paleomagnetic directions differ essentially: (1) 2A for the Gonam
Formation (Veselovsky et al., 2009) and 2B for the Konkuli and
Gonam formations (Pisarevsky, 2005) of the Uchur–Maya sedi-
mentary basin of the Aldan–Stanovoy province; (2) 3A (Veselovsky
et al., 2009) and 3B (Pisarevsky, 2005) for the Burdur Formation
of the Anabar massif; and (3) 4A (Veselovsky et al., 2009) and 4B
(Pisarevsky, 2005) for the Kotuikan Formation of the Anabar massif.
In Fig. 9a is shown the geographical position of the paleomagnetic
targets.
Reliability analysis of the paleomagnetic results is not
favourable for several reasons, the main being the accuracy of
determining the age of the paleomagnetic direction interpreted.
According to the available reliability criteria for paleomagnetic
measurements (e.g., Van der Voo, 1990; Pechersky and Didenko,
1995), results are considered valid if the accuracy of estimating the
age of rocks and the characteristic component of their NRM does
not exceed 20–30 Ma. In our set of specimens, only 17 independent
measurements were found to comply with the required accuracy
in determining the age (Fig. 9b; Table 3). One of them on the Kuon-
amka Dykes of the Anabar shield (Ernst et al., 2000), despite its

Of the remaining 16 measurements, two on rocks of the Baikal
ridge with an age of 1878 ± 4 Ma were excluded (Table 3, entries
25 and 26). The paleomagnetic directions of the two similar-age
rock formations and hence the positions of their paleomagnetic
poles calculated based on these directions differ significantly,
Fig. 9. Distribution of Paleoproterozoic and early Mesoproterozoic paleomagnetic
data on the Siberian platform (a) and accuracy of defining the age of the NRM
characteristic component (b). Solid (open) symbols mean reliable (unreliable) pale-

3.
is probably due to their formation outside a single tectoni-
cally rigid block; the difference of paleolatitudes is 11.1 ± 3.7◦and
the magnitude of the relative rotation is 27.5 ± 3.8◦. This agrees
with the conclusion made by Gladkochub et al. (2006): “Based
on the findings obtained as a result of studying indicator mafic-
ultramafic and granitoid complexes within the southern part of the
Siberian craton, it became possible to conclude that by ∼1.85 Ga
the formation of the southern Siberian craton structure had
completed”.
Thus, according to these two criteria only 14 measurements
remained (solid symbols in Figs. 9a and 10) to be used for fur-
ther analysis and generation of the APWP for Siberia at the end of
the Paleoproterozoic–beginning of the Mesoproterozoic. Most of
the data relates to the Angar–Anabar province (Akitkan and North
Baikal ridges, Sharyzhalgai and Angar–Kan salients of the Siberian
platform basement, Anabar massif) and only three measurements
to the Aldan–Stanovoy province (Fig. 9a), two of them being the
result of the present study (Table 3, entries 13 and 14) and one
belonging to Mikhailova et al. (1994) which is on anorthosites of
the Dzhugdzhur massif (Table 3, entry 16).
Two corrections were introduced for the purposes of the fur-
ther analysis. First, new positions of paleomagnetic poles of rock
formations from the Aldan–Stanovoy province by rotating them by
25◦counterclockwise about the rotation pole with the coordinates:
62◦N, 117◦E having regard to the rotation of the Aldan–Stanovoy
block relative to Angar–Anabar during the opening of the Vilyui rift
in the middle Paleozoic (Pavlov et al., 2008). In Table 3 and Fig. 10
they are marked with index “r”. Second, a minor age correction was
applied to the Khibelen (Table 3, entry 25) and Chaya (Table 3, entry
24) formations of the Akitkan ridge. The absolute geochronological
age (U–Pb, zircon) of the former is estimated at 1855 ± 4 Ma, and
that of the latter – 1863 ± 9 Ma (Didenko et al., 2009a,b; Vodovozov,
2010). In fact the Khibelen Formation is stratigraphically lower than
the Chaya Formation therefore to generate APWPs for them their
age was defined as 1859 and 1854 Ma, respectively, that is, in the
first case the maximum possible within the accuracy of determi-
nation and in the second case – the minimum possible within the
accuracy of determination. In Table 3 and Fig. 10 they are marked
with index “t”.
We believe it is necessary to specifically comment on the posi-
tion of the paleomagnetic poles obtained for the Ulkan massif
in the present study and anorthosites of the Dzhugdzhur massif
(Mikhailova et al., 1994).
Coordinates of the original pole of the Ulkan granitoid com-
plex (Plat = −42.1◦, Plong = 69.4◦, dp= 3.4◦, dm= 5.6◦) do not
coincide with the coordinates of the pole of the similar-age

### page_14
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 71
Fig. 10. Distribution of Paleoproterozoic and early Mezoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles of the Siberian platform. Solid (open) symbols mean reliable (unreliable) paleo-
magnetic poles (see text). Numbers on (a) correspond to numbers in Table 3. The APWP was generated by the cubic spline method (spline-factor is 5000) under the GMAP
programme (Torsvik and Smethurst, 1999). For the spline APWP coordinates see Table 4.
Angar–Kan granitoid block but after applying the correction for the
rotation of the Aldan–Stanovoy block relative to the Angar–Anabar
one in the middle Paleozoic (Pavlov et al., 2008) their positions
become very close (entries 13r and 15, Table 3; Fig. 10). Firstly,
this coincidence, in our opinion, is evidence in favour of the Pale-
oproterozoic age of the HTC of granites from the Ulkan complex.
Secondly, it suggests that the Ulkan block at the time of acquiring
the characteristic HTC of the NRM of granites from the Ulkan
complex was rigidly connected to the Angar–Anabar province.
Only in the Middle Paleozoic did they experience a significant
rotation relative to each other during the opening of the Vilyui
basin (aulacogen, rift) (Pavlov et al., 2008). The pole of the Ulkan
granites is used to generate the APWP for Siberia.
We see a different situation for paleomagnetic poles of
volcanogenic-sedimentary rocks of the Elgetey Formation (this
study) and anorthosites of the Dzhugdzhur massif (Mikhailova
et al., 1994). Their coordinates both before the rotation about the
above-mentioned pole of rotation (Table 3) and after the rotation
are in South Africa and far away from the similar-age granitoids
of the Angar–Kan block (entries 14r and 16r, Table 3; Fig. 10).
Given the paleomagnetic reliability of the poles under consider-
ation, we believe one can speak about tectonic incoherence of the
Ulkan and Dzhugdzhur massifs at ∼1732 Ma relative to the main
body of the Siberian craton, that is, the Angar–Anabar province.
Poles of volcanogenic-sedimentary rocks of the Elgetey Formation
(this study) and anorthosites of the Dzhugdzhur massif (Mikhailova
et al., 1994) are therefore not used in generating the APWP for
Siberia.
Positions of all the paleomagnetic poles from Table 3 are shown
in Fig. 10 after reversing them to one polarity according to the prin-
ciple of minimizing the movement. To the early Proterozoic poles
we added the pole position defined by Wingate et al. (2009), corre-
sponding to the beginning of the Mesoproterozoic (Table 3), with
the result that we get, in our opinion, a set of 12 most reliable
paleomagnetic poles to generate the late Paleoproterozoic–early
Mesoproterozoic segment of the APWP for Siberia. Analysis of
their distribution yields two clusters with reliably dated poles
(red numbers and solid symbols in Fig. 10): (1) 1840–1860 Ma
and (2) 1740–1470 Ma; within these clusters one can observe a
regular decrease in age of the poles directed in the branches of
the loop towards each other. Based on these 12 poles, the late
Paleoproterozoic–early Mesoproterozoic segment of the APWP for
Siberia was computer-calculated using the GMAP software (Torsvik
and Smethurst, 1999), which is shown by the solid line in Fig. 10,
and coordinates are listed in Table

5.2. Polarity and reconstructions of Siberia and Laurentia’ mutual
position
In contrast to Laurentia poles, to define polarity (normal or
reversal) for the Paleoproterozoic poles of Siberia is a challenge as
we lack a high-quality set of poles older than the late Precambrian.
There are gaps in one or more million years both for Neoproterozoic
and Mesoproterozoic times. Moreover, there are two alternative
models for the Neoproterozoic segment of the APWP for Siberia.
The first model was proposed by Smethurst et al. (1998), according
to which the Neoproterozoic normal polarity poles for Siberia occur
in temperate and tropical latitudes of the South Pacific (Fig. 11).
Later Shatsillo et al. (2005, 2006) reported new paleomagnetic data
on Vendian-Lower Cambrian sedimentary rocks of the southern

### page_15
72 A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77
Fig. 11. Comparison of the existing APWP with the one generated as a result of the study. Signs “N” and “S” for the spline APWP (this study) denote two possible variants
according to the accepted polarity (see text).
margin of Siberia and showed that corresponding paleomagnetic
poles of Siberia of this age are located in high, near Antarctica, and
temperate latitudes of the Indian Ocean. With this in mind it was
concluded: “The results of this study proved that the Vendian seg-
ment of the APWP for Siberia resided in the Indian Ocean and that
the earlier views concerning the Pacific trends of the Late Riphean
and Vendian poles were in error” (Shatsillo et al., 2006).
The second, alternative model of the Neoproterozoic segment
of the APWP for Siberia (Fig. 11) was proposed by Metelkin et al.
(2007). To construct the model, both original and published data
were used including the data obtained by Shatsillo et al. (2005,
2006). The position of the Neoproterozoic poles of normal polarity
according to Metelkin et al. (2007) is essentially different from that
defined by Smethurst et al. (1998). The second distinctive feature
of the trajectory drawn by Metelkin et al. (2007) is the loop which
both in age and shape is similar to the Grenvillian loop of the APWP
for Laurentia (Pisarevsky and Natapov, 2003).
As mentioned above, the model of the Mesoproterozoic seg-
ment of the APWP for Siberia has been proposed by Veselovsky
et al. (2009). According to this model, the corresponding normal
polarity poles are arranged in the subequatorial zone of the eastern
part of the Pacific (Fig. 11) and are, in fact, a continuation of the
Neoproterozoic track of the APWP (Smethurst et al., 1998).
An extended discussion of “pros and cons” of the above mod-
els of the APWP for Siberia is beyond the scope of this paper. The
main purpose of presenting these three models in the paper is
to highlight the fact that, as of now, there are no direct paleo-
magnetic data on polarity of the currently available paleomagnetic
poles for the second half of the Neoproterozoic, Mesoproterozoic
and, of course, Paleoproterozoic. To choose the option of polarity of
Siberia Paleoproterozoic and Mesoproterozoic poles, at this point,
we believe, non-paleomagnetic “tools”, such as geological, struc-
tural, geochronological, and others, should be used as it is shown
in a number of studies (e.g., Didenko et al., 2005; Pavlov et al., 2002;
Pisarevsky and Natapov, 2003) of which, in our case, a hypothesis of
the late Paleoproterozoic supercontinent, can be an example (e.g.,
Condie, 2002; Hoffman, 1997; Meert, 2002, 2012; Pesonen et al.,
2003; Piper, 2000; Zhao et al., 2002, 2004, 2011).
Possible positions of continental blocks in the structure of the
Proterozoic supercontinent based on the paleomagnetic data
subject
are
to ongoing discussions (e.g., Evans and Mitchell, 2011;
Pesonen et al., 2003; Pisarevsky et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012).
Siberia, whose possible positions relative to Laurentia at four time
periods are shown in Fig. 12, is no exception. Sign “N” denotes
an option when poles taken as northern are located in the North
Atlantic and North America, and sign “S” – in the Indian Ocean and
Australia (Fig. 11). Original poles were used in calculating positions
of Laurentia and Siberia (Fig. 12) with the exception of Siberia at
1590 Ma.
The following paleomagnetic poles were used to position
Laurentia (Fig. 12) at (1) 1840–1860 Ma from the A comp. of
the Wathaman batholith (Plat = 9, Plong = 293; Symons, 1991);
(2) 1730–1750 Ma from the A component of the Molson dykes
(Plat = −16, Plong = 277; Halls and Heaman, 2000) and Cleaver
dykes (Plat = 19, Plong = 277; Irving et al., 2004); and (3)
1590 Ma from dykes of Western Channel Diabase (WCD) (Plat = 9,
Plong = 245; Irving et al., 2004; age by Hamilton and Buchan,
2010); and (4) 1470–1480 Ma from the St. Francois Mtn. (Plat = −13,
Plong = 219; Meert and Stuckey, 2002). Usually normal polarity is
attributed to these poles, that is, they are northern, which is consis-
tent with the APWP for Laurentia constructed more than 20 years
ago (Piper, 1982), although there are alternative opinions (Park,
1994). Our constructions were also based on normal polarity of the
above mentioned poles of Laurentia, as the reverse polarity option
requires a more detailed analysis and revision of the existing set of
the Precambrian poles, which is not the subject of this paper.
The 1860–1840 Ma reconstructions place Laurentia in the north-
ern hemisphere, its modern northern edge being at 15–18◦ and
facing south (Fig. 12a). The position of Siberia calculated from the
coordinates of the paleomagnetic pole located in the Atlantic Ocean
is somewhat lower in latitude; it takes the equatorial position of
5◦N to 15◦S and its modern northern margin faces north towards
Laurentia (“N” on Fig. 12a). The paleocontinents are within 7–8◦.
In the case of the other polarity option when the north pole is in
the Indian Ocean, the position of Siberia will change by 180◦, that
is, the southern (Baikalian) margin of the Siberian craton will be by
the Arctic margin of Laurentia at 8–10◦N, and the two cratons will
be at a minimum distance (“S” on Fig. 12a).
We have the following position of the blocks at 1730–1750 Ma
(Fig. 12b) according to the pole from Halls and Heaman (2000).

### page_16
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 73
Fig. 12. Possible positions of Siberia relative to Laurentia according to the existing paleomagnetic poles 1840–1860 Ma (a), 1730–1750 Ma (b), 1740 ± 5 Ma (c), 1591 ± 4 Ma
(d) and 1470–1480 Ma (e). In (d) dashed line shows the position of Siberia and Laurentia considering the A95 confidence angle. Paleomagnetic poles used to calculate positions
of Laurentia and Siberia: (a) A comp. Wathaman batholiths – Plat = 9, Plong = 293 (Symons, 1991) and Shumikhinsky granites – Plat = −23.7, Plong = 94 (No. 23, Table 3); (b)
A comp. Molson dykes – Plat = −16, Plong = 277 (Halls and Heaman, 2000) and Angar–Kan granites – Plat = −42.9, Plong = 109 (No. 15, Table 3); (c) Cleaver dykes – Plat = 19,
Plong = 277 (Irving et al., 2004) and Angar–Kan granites – Plat = −42.9, Plong = 109 (No. 15, Table 3); (d) from dykes of Western Channel Diabase – Plat = 9, Plong = 245 (Irving
et al., 2004; age by Hamilton and Buchan, 2010) and the interpolated pole for Siberia (Table 4); (c) St. Francois Mtn., Plat = −13, Plong = 219 (Meert and Stuckey, 2002) and
Sololi intrusions (Wingate et al., 2009) – Plat = −33.6, Plong = 73.1 (No. 1, Table 3).
Laurentia moved by about 20◦ southward and simultaneously
rotated by 30–35◦counterclockwise. In the case of the north pole
location in the Atlantic Ocean Siberia will be entirely in the sube-
quatorial latitudes of the northern hemisphere from 5 to 30◦. The
orientation of Siberia remains virtually unchanged compared
its
to
position at 1840–1860 Ma. In this case, joining of Siberia and
Laurentia could occur along their current western margins as well
as modern eastern ones (“N” on Fig. 12b). In the case of the other
polarity option (north pole in the Indian Ocean) the position of
Siberia will change by 180◦, that is, the southern (Baikalian) edge

### page_17
74 A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77
Fig. 13. Reconstructions of Stanovoy (ST), Aldan (AL), and Angar–Anabar (AA) provinces of Siberia at 1732 Ma (left) and 1720 Ma (right). Star denotes the study area.
of Siberia will be by the modern Arctic margin of Laurentia at
5–8◦S and the Arctic one at 30◦S (“S” on Fig. 12b). In this case, the
present-day Arctic margin of Laurentia and the southern Baikalian
margin of Siberia could become adjacent, that is, their position is
not in conflict with the hypothesis of them being part of the super-
continent.
According to the Cleaver dykes pole (Irving et al., 2004), for
the same time period (1740 Ma) the position of Laurentia has not
changed much during the past 100 million years – it drifted north-
ward within 10◦ and rotated insignificantly counterclockwise. In
accordance with this pole, the present-day Arctic margin of Lau-
rentia was at 30◦N (Fig. 12c). The position of Siberia at this time
according to our data is described above. In such a situation, these
cratons could become adjacent along their present-day Arctic mar-
gins only provided that the north pole (normal polarity) for Siberia
is in the Atlantic (Fig. 12c, option “N”). In the case that the North
Pole is in the Indian Ocean, there had to be a gap as wide as 30◦
(Fig. 12c, option “S”).
The WCD pole (Irving et al., 2004) and age interpretation after
(Hamilton and Buchan, 2010; Buchan, 2014) for Laurentia and the
interpolated pole for Siberia (Table 4) due to the lack of reliable
data for this interval (Table 3), were used to reconstruct the mutual
position of the two cratons at 1590 Ma (Fig. 12d). At this time, Lau-
rentia was entirely in the northern hemisphere, its Arctic margin
in the tropical latitudes of 10–25◦ facing the south-east. Siberia,
in the case of the north pole being in the Atlantic Ocean, will be
entirely in the subequatorial latitudes of the northern hemisphere
from 0 to 20◦, its Arctic margin facing the north-west towards the
Arctic margin of Laurentia (Fig. 12d, option “N”). In the case of the
other polarity option (north pole in the Indian Ocean), the posi-
tion of Siberia will change by 180◦and will be in the subequatorial
latitudes of the southern hemisphere. The “Baikalian” margin of
Siberia will face the north-west towards the Arctic margin of Lau-
rentia (Fig. 12d, option “S”). In the latter case there is a latitudinal
gap of about 15◦ between the Arctic margin of Laurentia and the
“Baikalian” margin of Siberia. But considering A95 = 6◦(confidence
limit) for the Laurentia original pole; Irving et al., 2004) and similar
A95 values for the Siberia interpolated pole one can significantly
bring together these cratons and “close” the gap (Fig. 12d, dashed
line).
We have the following position of the blocks at 1470–1480 Ma
(Fig. 12e). Laurentia moved by about 10◦ further south rotating
at the same time by approximately 20◦ counterclockwise. Siberia
in the case of the north pole being in the Atlantic Ocean will be
entirely in the subequatorial latitudes of the northern hemisphere
from 0 to 20◦(Fig. 12e, option “N”). In the case of the other polarity
option (northern pole in the Indian Ocean), the position of Siberia
will change by 180◦, and again the southern (Baikalian) margin
Siberia
of
will be contiguous with the present-day Arctic margin of
Laurentia (Fig. 12e, option “S”).
If we proceed from the assumption that Laurentia, Siberia,
Baltica, India and Australia started joining 1.80 Ga ago (Zhang
et al., 2012), then one combination – the modern southern edge
of Siberia is close to the modern Arctic edge of Laurentia –
occurs in three reconstructions at 1840–1860, 1730–1750 and
1470–1480 Ma (Fig. 12a, b, and e). Such fit is not observed in the
fourth reconstruction at ca. 1590 Ma, but the difference is not crit-
ical. Taking into account the confidence intervals, one can achieve
an acceptable position of the cratons when the southern margin of
Siberia is contiguous with the Arctic margin of Laurentia (Fig. 12d).
Such a joint presence of Siberia and Laurentia in the structure
of the Paleoproterozoic supercontinent is referred to not only in
Zhang et al. (2012), where our paleomagnetic data on the Akitkan
ridge are used (Didenko et al., 2009a,b), but also in Condie (2002)
based on the analysis of geological and isotopic-geochronological
data on the end of the late Proterozoic. The same relative posi-
tion of the two paleocontinents at the turn of the Meso- and
Neoproterozoic considering the available geological, structural and
isotopic-geochemical data is referred to in Rainbird et al. (1998)
and considering the paleomagnetic data in Pavlov et al. (2002)
and Metelkin et al. (2012), and on the basis of matching the LIP
record between southern Siberia and northern Laurentia (Ernst
et al., 2014).
The 1740 Ma reconstruction (Fig. 12c) wherein the position of
Laurentia is calculated according to the Cleaver dykes pole (Irving
et al., 2004) and the latitudinal gap between the cratons can hardly
be “removed” by applying correction for A95 values. We are not
able to give a reasonable explanation as the analysis of Paleopro-
terozoic paleomagnetic poles of Laurentia is beyond the scope of
this paper, on the one hand, and on the other, without know-
ing the detailed geology of Laurentia in the Paleoproterozoic it
is unlikely that the authors of this paper are capable of doing it.
The only thing worth mentioning here is the presence of at least
two (high- and low-latitudinal) groups of paleomagnetic poles in
the interval 1850–1740 Ma for Laurentia, which are similar in their
meridional position but differ appreciably in their latitudinal posi-
tion (see Table 1 in Pesonen et al., 2003). The Cleaver dykes pole
(Irving et al., 2004) has approximately the same meridional posi-
tion and the latitudinal position, which is intermediate between
the high- and low-latitudinal groups.
On the strength of the data presented here, one can conclude
that in the context of the Paleoproterozoic supercontinent model,
preference is given to the position of Paleoproterozoic north poles
of Siberia in the Indian Ocean and Australia (APWP “S” in Fig. 11),
rather than in the Atlantic Ocean (APWP “N” in Fig. 11). This con-
clusion is valid if we adhere to the accepted polarity option for the

### page_18
A.N. Didenko et al. / Precambrian Research 259 (2015) 58–77 75
Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles of Laurentia (Piper, 1982)
which is also used in (Pesonen et al., 2003; Pisarevsky et al., 2014).
6. Position of the Ulkan massif
Paleomagnetic data on the Paleoproterozoic Ulkan massif made
it possible to derive two ancient paleomagnetic directions, close
in time of formation to the rocks under study, and to calculate
the corresponding paleomagnetic poles for two sections of the late
Paleoproterozoic – 1732 Ma for volcanogenic-sedimentary rocks of
the Elgetey Formation (positive fold, reversals, and conglomerates
tests) and less than 1720 Ma for granites of the Ulkan Complex.
According to our data and comparison with the APWP for Siberia
(see the previous part), at the time of the studied rocks forma-
tion the Ulkan massif was located at 18–26◦S. The massif rotated
about the vertical axis by 70 ± 8◦ clockwise 1732 Ma (age of the
Elgetey Formation) and ∼1720 Ma (age of the HTC of the Ulkan
granites) ago (Figure 13). At 1732 Ma the Ulkan massif and other
terranes of Angar–Anabar and Aldan–Stanovoy provinces were
located in the southern tropical latitude close to one another. Dur-
ing ∼12 Myr both blocks shifted northward by an average of 5◦. The
Angar–Anabar block retained its azimuth orientation, whereas the
Ulkan massif (maybe the Aldan–Stanovoy block) experienced sig-
nificance clockwise rotation and became tectonically coherent to
Siberia ∼1720 Ma ago.
7. Conclusions
Paleomagnetic studies on Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Ulkan
trough yielded two ancient paleomagnetic directions and made
it possible to calculate poles corresponding to them for two
time intervals in the late Paleoproterozoic: (ɑ) ∼1732 Ma for
volcanogenic-sedimentary rocks of the Elgetey Formation –
Plat = 7.1◦ (−7.1◦), Plong = 183.5◦ (3.5◦), dp= 10.5, dm= 16.4◦ (pos-
itive fold test); and (b) less than 1720 Ma for granites of the Ulkan
Complex – Plat = 42.1◦ (−42.1◦), Plong = 249.4◦ (69.4◦), dp= 3.4◦,
dm= 5.6◦.
The analysis of the existing paleomagnetic data for Siberia in
late Paleoproterozoic–early Mesoproterozoic times allowed 12 key
poles to be defined (Table 3), based on which the APWP for Siberia
was generated (Fig. 11; Table 4).
We can conclude that in the context of the Paleoproterozoic
supercontinent model, preference is given to the position of Paleo-
proterozoic north poles of Siberia in the Indian Ocean and Australia,
rather than in the Atlantic Ocean.
According to the new paleomagnetic data and comparison with
the APWP for Siberia, at the time of the studied rocks formation
the Ulkan massif was located at 18–26◦S. The massif rotated about
the vertical axis by 70 ± 8◦ clockwise 1.732 Ga (age of the Elgetey
Formation) and ≤1.72 Ga (age of the HTC of the Ulkan granites) ago.
